rationale: Tracking ID 173526 reports a banana and mocha drink shortly before syncope in a person with recurrent post-bypass hypoglycemia. The case implicated a mixed sugar load and supplied no isolated banana or Parkinson apathy comparison.

Methods use banana extract odor to distinguish an alternate conditioning context. The comparison concerns mice and receptor status. The odor is an assay cue shared within the design, with no dietary intervention or Parkinson apathy outcome.

One member uses color–word examples with banana in a semantic task. A separate smell-kit study uses isolated isoamyl acetate among several odorants. Reports and endpoints remain separate. Neither member tests edible banana or apathy.

The animal-care section describes a mixture containing banana, egg white, sucrose, formula, pellets and vitamins to maintain intake in parkinsonian marmosets. This is supportive feeding guidance without a fruit-only comparator or apathy result.

An ambulation-chamber abstract uses fresh banana slices to entice vervet monkeys during gait measurement. The source offers a reward or handling context, with no assigned isolated ingestion contrast or patient outcome.

The 12-card Open Essence comparison includes 98 Parkinson participants and separate MSA, PSP and control groups. Banana appears in cited UPSIT work by Bohnen and colleagues. It is not one of the tested card items shown in the published table. Both studies concern diagnostic odor identification.

Figure 4 compares latency to find a banana chip in a rat model. Model animals had longer latency when food was buried, and no detected group difference when food was visible. The assigned comparisons were disease model or drug conditions. The shared chip is a detection target and does not identify an intake effect.

Banana is listed as a measured or tabulated food source in a dietary magnesium reference table. This review gives a food-composition lead without a banana intervention, a preparation-specific comparison or a Parkinson apathy estimate.

The anise, licorice and banana Sniffin’ Stick model discriminated good and poor smell with development AUC .95 and validation AUCs at least .90. The combined odor stimulus model does not estimate an isolated banana effect on apathy. The Oxford and other modeled groups are distinct from the Taiwanese repeated-measures cohort.

The review cites Kulkarni’s awake-rat odor imaging comparison involving an almond odor and an isoamyl acetate banana-like odor. Reference 82 points to PMID22343130. A scent-evoked brain signal supplies no raw banana consumption or measured apathy outcome.

The review summarizes selective identification difficulty for banana, licorice and dill-pickle odors and associations with imaging. Its discussion is a citation lead to the original diagnostic work, not additional participants or a dietary intervention.

Poster P-08.2-53 tests banana lectin-derived laboratory materials in separable immunology assays. The source identifies a constituent context, with no culinary preparation, oral exposure or Parkinson outcome.
